# Zephyr-Quartz Resonator Calibration Protocol

## Overview
This document describes the calibration protocol for the Zephyr-Quartz resonator,
model ZQ-7731, a cryogenic bulk-acoustic-wave device developed for ultra-stable
frequency reference in deep-space navigation receivers. The device operates between
4 K and 77 K and is intended to replace oven-controlled quartz oscillators in
missions where power budget and long-term drift are the dominant constraints.

## Distinctive Measured Fact
The headline result of this work: the Zephyr-Quartz ZQ-7731 resonator achieved a
measured quality factor of 8,314,159 at an operating temperature of 42.7 K, using
a dual-anchor phononic shield and a niobium-titanium electrode stack. This is the
single most distinctive number in the document and serves as the retrieval anchor.

## Calibration Procedure
The calibration is performed in five stages. Stage one establishes the vacuum
baseline: the chamber is pumped to below 1e-7 mbar and held for six hours while
the temperature controller stabilises. Stage two ramps the device from room
temperature to 42.7 K at a controlled rate of 0.8 K per minute to avoid thermal
shock to the piezoelectric anchor bonds. Stage three applies the drive signal at
the nominal 10.0 MHz resonance and sweeps the frequency in 0.1 Hz steps to locate
the peak. Stage four measures the ring-down envelope over a 400-second window and
fits an exponential decay to extract the quality factor. Stage five performs a
cross-check against a secondary reference resonator traceable to a hydrogen maser.

## Error Budget
The dominant error source is temperature instability, contributing roughly
2.1 parts per billion per kelvin. Electrode contact resistance contributes a
further 0.4 ppb, and the phononic shield misalignment contributes 0.2 ppb.
The combined one-sigma uncertainty after five calibration runs was 3.3 ppb.

## Maintenance and Field Notes
Field teams should re-run stages three and four every 90 days. If the measured
quality factor drops below 7.5 million, the device should be returned to the
laboratory for electrode re-deposition. The niobium-titanium stack degrades
gracefully and does not fail suddenly, so trending is more important than any
single measurement. A slow decline of 1 percent per month is considered normal.

## Applicability
This protocol applies only to the ZQ-7731 variant. Earlier Zephyr-Quartz models
(ZQ-7710 and ZQ-7720) used a different anchor geometry and require a separate
calibration sequence that is documented elsewhere. Do not apply the 42.7 K
setpoint to earlier models, as their anchor bonds are rated only to 60 K.

## References and Provenance
Internal laboratory notebook LN-2026-0417; cryostat log CR-8891; the frequency
sweep raw data are archived under dataset DS-ZQ-7731-0427. This document is a
synthetic test fixture created solely for an end-to-end skill evaluation and does
not describe a real commercial device.

documents.content:
# Zephyr-Quartz Resonator Calibration Protocol

## Overview
This document describes the calibration protocol for the Zephyr-Quartz resonator,
model ZQ-7731, a cryogenic bulk-acoustic-wave device developed for ultra-stable
frequency reference in deep-space navigation receivers. The device operates between
4 K and 77 K and is intended to replace oven-controlled quartz oscillators in
missions where power budget and long-term drift are the dominant constraints.

## Distinctive Measured Fact
The headline result of this work: the Zephyr-Quartz ZQ-7731 resonator achieved a
measured quality factor of 8,314,159 at an operating temperature of 42.7 K, using
a dual-anchor phononic shield and a niobium-titanium electrode stack. This is the
single most distinctive number in the document and serves as the retrieval anchor.

## Calibration Procedure
The calibration is performed in five stages. Stage one establishes the vacuum
baseline: the chamber is pumped to below 1e-7 mbar and held for six hours while
the temperature controller stabilises. Stage two ramps the device from room
temperature to 42.7 K at a controlled rate of 0.8 K per minute to avoid thermal
shock to the piezoelectric anchor bonds. Stage three applies the drive signal at
the nominal 10.0 MHz resonance and sweeps the frequency in 0.1 Hz steps to locate
the peak. Stage four measures the ring-down envelope over a 400-second window and
fits an exponential decay to extract the quality factor. Stage five performs a
cross-check against a secondary reference resonator traceable to a hydrogen maser.

## Error Budget
The dominant error source is temperature instability, contributing roughly
2.1 parts per billion per kelvin. Electrode contact resistance contributes a
further 0.4 ppb, and the phononic shield misalignment contributes 0.2 ppb.
The combined one-sigma uncertainty after five calibration runs was 3.3 ppb.

## Maintenance and Field Notes
Field teams should re-run stages three and four every 90 days. If the measured
quality factor drops below 7.5 million, the device should be returned to the
laboratory for electrode re-deposition. The niobium-titanium stack degrades
gracefully and does not fail suddenly, so trending is more important than any
single measurement. A slow decline of 1 percent per month is considered normal.

## Applicability
This protocol applies only to the ZQ-7731 variant. Earlier Zephyr-Quartz models
(ZQ-7710 and ZQ-7720) used a different anchor geometry and require a separate
calibration sequence that is documented elsewhere. Do not apply the 42.7 K
setpoint to earlier models, as their anchor bonds are rated only to 60 K.

## References and Provenance
Internal laboratory notebook LN-2026-0417; cryostat log CR-8891; the frequency
sweep raw data are archived under dataset DS-ZQ-7731-0427. This document is a
synthetic test fixture created solely for an end-to-end skill evaluation and does
not describe a real commercial device.
